title: Entropy Increases with Increasing Temperature
lead: The first and second laws together give the internal energy and the enthalpy as functions of entropy, and the heat capacities then tell how the entropy of a substance changes as it is heated at constant volume or at constant pressure.
objectives: Define entropy and its relation to energy flow.
notes: The page names no authors, and Example 21.1.1, printed without a solution, is set as an exercise.
exercise_notes: Example 21.1.1, which the book prints as five steps with no solution, is unkeyed and has an AI solution; its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Problem 1 of the chapter's exercise page (21.E), routed here, is unkeyed and has an AI solution, its answer computed; its Bloom level and concept tag were chosen by AI.

exercises.prompt:
1. Write $\kU$ as a function of $\kT$ and $\kV$.
  2. Write $\kU$ as a function of its natural variables.
  3. Rearrange (2) to find an expression for $d\kSent$.
  4. Substitute (1) into (3) and rearrange. This is the definition of $\kCV$.
  5. Write out $\kSent$ as a function of $\kT$ and $\kV$.

answer.hint: Write the total differential of $U(T, V)$ and set it equal to $T\,dS - P\,dV$.
answer.solution:
(1) As a function of $\kT$ and $\kV$, $d\kU = \left(\dfrac{\partial \kU}{\partial \kT}\right)_{\kV} d\kT + \left(\dfrac{\partial \kU}{\partial \kV}\right)_{\kT} d\kV$.

(2) In its natural variables, $d\kU = \kT\,d\kSent - \kP\,d\kV$.

(3) Solved for the entropy, $d\kSent = \dfrac{1}{\kT}\,d\kU + \dfrac{\kP}{\kT}\,d\kV$.

(4) Putting (1) into (3) gives $d\kSent = \dfrac{1}{\kT}\left(\dfrac{\partial \kU}{\partial \kT}\right)_{\kV} d\kT + \dfrac{1}{\kT}\left[\left(\dfrac{\partial \kU}{\partial \kV}\right)_{\kT} + \kP\right] d\kV$. The coefficient of $d\kT$ is $(\partial \kSent/\partial \kT)_{\kV}$, so $\left(\dfrac{\partial \kSent}{\partial \kT}\right)_{\kV} = \dfrac{1}{\kT}\left(\dfrac{\partial \kU}{\partial \kT}\right)_{\kV} = \dfrac{\kCV}{\kT}$, which is the definition of $\kCV$ written as $\kCV = \kT(\partial \kSent/\partial \kT)_{\kV}$.

(5) For $\kSent(\kT, \kV)$, then, $d\kSent = \dfrac{\kCV}{\kT}\,d\kT + \dfrac{1}{\kT}\left[\left(\dfrac{\partial \kU}{\partial \kV}\right)_{\kT} + \kP\right] d\kV$. At constant volume only the first term is left, which is $d\kSent = (\kCV/\kT)\,d\kT$.

exercises.source_id: Liquid water has a nearly constant molar heat capacity
exercises.prompt: Liquid water has a nearly constant molar heat capacity of $\bar{C}_P=75.4.\;\text{J}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. What is the change in entropy as 200. g of water are cooled from 70.0°C to 20.0°C?

answer.hint: With a constant heat capacity the integral of $C_P/T$ is $nC_P\ln(T_2/T_1)$, in kelvins.
answer.solution: The water is $n = 200.\ \text{g}/18.015\ \text{g mol}^{-1} = 11.10$ mol. With $\bar{C}_P$ constant, $\Delta \kSent = \displaystyle\int_{\kTone}^{\kTtwo} \dfrac{n\bar{C}_P}{\kT}\,d\kT = n\bar{C}_P\ln\dfrac{\kTtwo}{\kTone}$, and the temperatures are $\kTone = 343.15$ K and $\kTtwo = 293.15$ K. So $\Delta \kSent = (11.10\ \text{mol})(75.4\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})\ln\dfrac{293.15}{343.15} = (837.1\ \text{J/K})(-0.1575) = -131.8$ J/K. The entropy falls because the water is cooled.
